newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhs losing patience over wage, pension arrears.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhs losing patience over wage, pension arrears.

text.p: School teachers in Kazakhstan threatened strike action and energy workers went on hunger strike on Tuesday over wage arrears despite government promises to pay salaries and pensions.

In Karaganda, a large coal and steel producing town in the centre of the former Soviet republic, 50 workers at one the town's power plants began a hunger strike in protest over wages which have not been paid for five months.
The plant's director, Gennady Shatsky, told Reuters it was the second such protest since December.
School teachers in Kazakhstan's hard-hit northern regions have threatened to start an open-ended strike from Thursday if the government failed to pay their salaries.
Teachers in the grain-producing Kostonai region have not yet received salaries for June 1996, said Lyudmila Semyenova of the republic's Trade Union of People's Education.
She said the government owed teachers around six billion tenge (about $80 million) in back pay.
"The government takes advantage of our patience and say they will act," said Semyenova. "This patience is running out."

The huge backlog of unpaid wages and pensions prompted Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev last week to threaten government and regional officials with dismissal if they failed to find a solution to the payments crisis by April 1.

Alexander Pavlov, the republic's finance minister, put the blame on laggardly tax collection, "mad" policies by regional chiefs and the slow pace of privatisation for the dizzying backlog of unpaid wages and pensions.
"The largest debts for salaries are in education," Pavlov told a news conference in the capital Almaty. "But we will use our grain, metals, oil and gas to help pay wages," he said.
The minister said the regions would be given strict timetables to pay employees at hospitals and schools.
Pavlov added the payment of wages and pensions would not, as some observers fear, fuel inflation.
"There is no danger the tenge will fall," he said. Kazakhstan is committed to stringent market reforms sponsored by the International Monetary Fund.
President Nazarabyev, with strong executive powers, tolerates only limited dissent in the Central Asian republic, rich in oil and gas.
There have been no large-scale demonstrations among the 16.9 million population like those in other east European states despite severe economic hardship since independence from Moscow in 1991.
But as Pavlov was speaking, a noisy group of pensioners stood on the icy steps of the government building in Almaty demanding a meeting and explanation from ministers over their own pension arrears.
"All our lives we built this," said 64-year-old Irina Savostina, head of the Generation lobby group for pensioners, waving her arms at the city, sparkling in the winter sun.
"Now they try and suffocate us," she said, complaining that her 4,000 tenge ($52) pension, even if it was paid, only fed her for a week.
